ExplanationParts.CorpusEarnedOpening: Eating rice when hungry recurs as an answer, self-description, quotation, and point of public criticism, usually paired with sleeping when tired.
EvidenceBody: Huanglong Huinan places it in a four-action series: eat when hungry, sleep when tired, approach fire when cold, and take coolness when hot. Dahui Zonggao quotes Lingzhao’s reply, ‘neither hard nor easy—when hungry, eat rice; when tired, sleep,’ and appraises the Pang family as walking together but not in step. Yuanwu Keqin uses a graphic variant beside ordinary mind, and Dongshan Zhiqian uses it in a self-description. Dazhu Huihai supplies the decisive contrast: other people refuse simply to eat or sleep and instead make a hundred demands and a thousand calculations. Hongzhi Zhengjue likewise says the monastery manager knows only eating when hungry and does not know the many kinds of affairs. The ordinary meal becomes interview language, but the records prevent mere repetition from settling the matter.

DraftEvidence.ZenBend: “When hungry, eat rice” recurs as an answer and self-description, while Dazhu Huihai explicitly distinguishes his eating from the distracted eating attributed to other people.
